summary: This document describes a way for DNS operators to update DNSSEC delegation trust information using the DNS itself as the communication channel. It targets cases where moving key information from a child zone to its parent is currently hard, such as when rolling Key Signing Keys.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7344 lets a child DNS zone publish the DNSSEC key information it wants its parent to use. The parent can retrieve and check that information instead of relying only on manual exchanges.

questions: how to roll dnssec ksk with parent
what are cds and cdnskey records
how to automate dnssec ds updates
how does a double ds ksk rollover work
subtitle: How a child DNS zone can publish desired delegation key data for its parent.

tldr.problem: Changing DNSSEC keys often requires sending updated information from a child zone to its parent through a manual process that can be missed or entered incorrectly.
tldr.mechanism: The child publishes CDS or CDNSKEY records that describe the desired DS data at the parent. A parental agent retrieves and validates those records before changing the parent's DS set.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7344 describes automation of later DS updates, not initial key enrollment or removal of all keys. The unit metadata lists RFC 8078, RFC 9615, and RFC 9975 as updates.

today: RFC 7344 identifies itself as an Informational RFC. The unit metadata lists RFC 8078, RFC 9615, and RFC 9975 as updates.

sections.title: The Problem with Delegation Key Changes
sections.content:
When a child zone first signs its data, its key information must reach the parent to establish the DNSSEC chain of trust. Each later key change also requires the parent to update its records. The RFC notes that this exchange is often manual and can lead to errors or skipped updates.

RFC 7344 uses DNS publication as a channel for automating later DS changes. It does not cover the first key enrollment or removing all keys. It also covers DNSSEC key data, not other delegation information such as NS and glue records.
sections.plainLanguage: When a child changes its DNSSEC key, the parent must update its delegation data. Publishing the desired change in DNS can reduce manual exchanges.

sections.title: The Parent, Child, and Parental Agent
sections.content:
The Child is the delegated domain, and the Parent is the domain in which it is registered. The Child DNS Operator maintains the child's zone. The Parental Agent is the entity the child contacts to change delegation information.

The parent can publish a DS record set that identifies DNSKEY records the child uses to sign its DNSKEY record set. This forms the chain Parent DNSKEY → DS → Child DNSKEY. The child and parent may communicate directly, through an API or web interface, or through intermediaries. The method is aimed at cases where their operations are separate.
sections.plainLanguage: The child publishes its zone, while the parent publishes information about the delegation. A parental agent handles the parent's side of a key change.

sections.title: CDS and CDNSKEY Records
sections.content:
The RFC defines two DNS resource record types. CDS has the same wire and presentation format as DS and describes the DS record set the child wants at the parent. CDNSKEY has the same format as DNSKEY and carries child DNSKEY records for the parent to process. Their assigned type codes are 59 and 60.

The records express the desired replacement set, not a list of individual additions and deletions. Software consuming CDNSKEY can calculate DS records. Authoritative servers and resolvers do not perform special processing for either type. If neither record set is present, no change is requested.

Use is OPTIONAL. A child SHOULD publish both types if it publishes either, unless it knows which one its parent consumes. If it publishes both, their contents MUST match.
sections.plainLanguage: CDS and CDNSKEY records state what key information the child wants the parent to publish. They describe the complete desired set, rather than individual changes.

sections.title: How a Parent Checks and Applies an Update
sections.content:
A CDS or CDNSKEY record MUST be at the child zone apex. It MUST be signed with a key represented in both current DNSKEY and DS sets, except when a parent uses another method to validate initial enrollment. Applying the record MUST NOT break the current delegation. The parent MUST ignore records that fail these checks and SHOULD log the error.

The parent chooses CDS or CDNSKEY as its default and MUST NOT assume the child publishes both. It can poll signed children or fetch records after a trigger. A parental agent SHOULD use a DNSSEC validator and MUST make sure an older record set does not overwrite a newer one. If no CDS or CDNSKEY set exists, it MUST NOT change or delete the current DS set.

A parent that consumes CDNSKEY can calculate the DS set in full mode, publishing only the DS records it computes, or augment mode, ensuring records for digest algorithms it requires.
sections.plainLanguage: The parent checks that the update is in the right place, signed by an accepted key, and safe for the existing delegation. If no update is published, the parent leaves its DS records alone.

sections.title: A Double-DS Key Rollover
sections.content:
The appendix shows a Key Signing Key rollover from key A to key B using the Double-DS method. First the child publishes CDS records containing both keys. After the parent publishes both DS records and the DS time-to-live has passed, the child switches to key B.

After the DNSKEY time-to-live has passed, the child removes key A from CDS. The parent then removes the old DS record, and the child may optionally delete its CDS records. The wait steps let old information expire from caches before the next change.
sections.plainLanguage: The example keeps the old and new keys represented during the change. The child switches to the new key only after the parent and cached records have had time to catch up.

sections.title: Security Limits and Recovery
sections.content:
This automation cannot repair every failure. If the child removes all DNSKEYs represented in the parent's DS set, it must contact the parent or restore those keys. If the child's signing system is compromised, an attacker may publish CDS or CDNSKEY records and extend the attack. Delaying acceptance can give the operator time to detect a change.

The RFC says the method SHOULD NOT be used for initial key enrollment because it cannot establish that the first key is correct. If it is used for enrollment, strict validation rules and a challenge mechanism MUST be used. An empty CDS or CDNSKEY set means no change; it cannot remove all keys to make a zone unsigned.

The RFC says the information handled is public DNS data. It also notes that a third-party DNS provider can maintain DNSSEC information without receiving a registrant's registrar credentials.
sections.plainLanguage: This method is for changing established delegation data, not safely choosing the first key. A compromised signing system can publish false updates, so parents still need careful checks.
